vignette:
She cannot remember the sound of the collapse itself—only the way the air changed. One moment she was standing at the back of the community hall, nodding to the chief engineer as he presented the renovation timeline for the old Riverside School. The next, every breath was full of dust, and the floor beneath her feet had become a chaos of splintered wood and twisted metal. The lights died. Then the screaming started.

That was fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in early autumn. She was thirty-one then, newly elected to the city council, proud of the infrastructure subcommittee she had fought to chair. The East Wing collapse killed six people: three adults—two maintenance workers and a parent volunteer—and three children from the after-school program. No one had ever proven that the contractor cut corners on the beam supports, but the forensic report made it clear the failure was human, not accidental. Man-made. She still sees the face of the ten-year-old girl who was found under the piano, still hears the mother’s voice on the news footage that played for weeks.

In the months after, she stopped going to public works meetings. She told her chief of staff it was a scheduling conflict, but really her chest tightened every time she walked past the elevators in City Hall. Concrete walls made her feel trapped. She started taking the stairs, even for the seventh floor, even when her knees ached. At night, she sees the collapse in slow motion, the ceiling bowing inward like a held breath. She wakes up gasping, convinced she is buried. Her apartment is on the third floor now; she moved from a high-rise because she could not stand the sound of the elevator cables.

At work, she fights for stricter building codes with an intensity that puzzles her colleagues. She drafts motions about load-bearing inspections and emergency evacuation drills. But when she stands at the dais during council meetings, the faces in the audience blur. She loses her place in her notes. The hush of the room feels like the moment before the fall. She has stopped attending public hearings, sending her legislative aide instead. Last month, she snapped at a constituent who asked about the school rebuild; the woman had meant well, but the question turned her hands cold and her voice brittle. She apologized later, but the damage felt done.

Her mother calls from Bangalore every Sunday. She asks about marriage, about whether she is eating properly. She tells her daughter she works too hard. Her daughter cannot explain that she is afraid to go grocery shopping alone because the fluorescent lights hum in a way that reminds her of the emergency sirens. She cannot say that the smell of wet concrete at a construction site makes her nauseous. So she says she is fine, and her mother says, “You sound tired,” and they hang up.

She has not visited the Riverside School memorial. She knows exactly where it is, at the corner of the playground where the new garden was planted. She takes a different route to work now, looping three blocks out of her way. When someone mentions the anniversary of the collapse in the office, she leaves the room without excusing herself. The guilt is a constant low buzz: if she had pushed harder on the contractor audit, if she had questioned the timeline, if she had been standing somewhere else, if she had been able to reach the children in the seconds before the dust settled. Her therapist has asked her to write the story of that day. She started it seven times. Each time, she stops before the ceiling falls.
